title: Japan's Rare Earth Squeeze Deepens as China Keeps Heavy Minerals Tap Shut
subhead: Japanese materials makers are drawing down inventories as dysprosium and yttrium imports fall roughly 80% from two years ago, while Washington authorizes private security firms to conduct offensive cyber operations against overseas hackers.

sections.heading: Japan's Rare Earth Squeeze Deepens
sections.body: Japan is finding it increasingly hard to source rare earths for electric vehicles and chipmaking equipment as Chinese trade restrictions squeeze supplies, according to Nikkei Asia. The outlet reports that imports of dysprosium and yttrium have plummeted around 80% compared with two years ago, forcing Japanese materials companies to draw down rare-earth inventories to keep delivering to major customers. The squeeze follows Beijing cutting Japan off from several heavy rare earths and other materials for at least four months, a move Reuters reported in May coincided with a dispute between the two countries over Taiwan. China sent no gallium, dysprosium, terbium or yttrium to Japan in June, per reporting cited by Vozpópuli, and Reuters noted China's heavy rare earth exports to Japan stayed tiny again in July.
sections.whyItMatters: Heavy rare earths are essential for EV magnets and precision chipmaking tools, so the sustained cutoff is a direct test of how far Beijing will use mineral leverage in a Taiwan-linked dispute — and how quickly Japan can diversify away from Chinese supply.

sections.heading: Washington Authorizes Private Firms to Hack Overseas Cybercriminals
sections.body: In a National Security Presidential Memorandum issued Thursday, President Donald Trump directed the National Coordination Center to develop a program for conducting cyber operations against foreign transnational criminal organizations, and the lynchpin is bringing in private-sector security firms, Ars Technica reports. The memo, which the White House says is the first time the federal government will authorize private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against overseas hackers, lists ransomware, sextortion, phishing, financial fraud and impersonation scams as eligible targets. The Departments of Justice and Homeland Security will provide oversight. The memo does not rule out offensive attacks that use encryption to lock targets out of networks or distributed denial-of-service operations, Ars Technica notes.
sections.whyItMatters: This shifts a traditionally government-only capability — offensive hacking — into the private sector, raising new questions about accountability, collateral damage and how far firms can go against targets that are not clearly state-affiliated.

sections.heading: US and South Korea Warn of Gunra Ransomware
sections.body: US federal agencies and South Korea's National Policy Agency issued a joint advisory warning government and critical infrastructure organizations worldwide to secure systems against Gunra ransomware, BleepingComputer reports. The advisory says Gunra first emerged in April 2025 as a double-extortion variant derived from the leaked Conti ransomware source code, and has been observed exploiting two critical authentication vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy (CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472) to gain footholds. Since January 2026, Gunra has launched a formal ransomware-as-a-service affiliate program on dark web forums, adopted the alias Golden Community, and begun recruiting initial access brokers, the joint advisory says. The FBI observed the group emailing victim management directly to solicit ransom payments.
sections.whyItMatters: Gunra's shift to a RaaS model with cross-platform (Windows and Linux) payloads and active broker recruitment signals a more industrialized threat aimed squarely at government and critical infrastructure — exactly the sectors the joint advisory targets.

sections.heading: Memory Makers Flush With Cash as AI Capacity Race Intensifies
sections.body: Memory manufacturers are reaping the benefits of the flood of AI spending by US tech giants, with Nikkei Asia reporting the sector is flush with roughly $90 billion in cash flow that is being plowed into capacity investment. Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung are lining up big capacity expansions, while Kioxia plays catch-up, Nikkei reports. The investment wave comes as AI demand keeps memory prices elevated — Nikkei separately reported that Japan's used iPhone and server sales have surged as memory prices soar, with refurbished model sales more than doubling after Apple price hikes.
sections.whyItMatters: The memory boom is funding a new round of capacity buildout that will shape who controls the HBM and DRAM supply that AI training and inference depend on — and it is lifting the whole sector, including China's CXMT, which Nikkei reported has become China's most valuable company.

sections.heading: China's Foundries and Equipment Makers Keep Selling Into the AI Boom
sections.body: China's top contract chipmaker SMIC says AI 'spillover effects' are boosting prices for peripheral chips, and it will not lower prices for other sectors despite weak smartphone and auto markets, Nikkei Asia reports. Separately, US equipment maker Applied Materials projects its China revenue will grow in 2026 despite US export curbs, after reporting record earnings driven by AI demand, per Nikkei. The two reports together show the AI-driven chip cycle is lifting both Chinese foundries and American equipment suppliers that keep selling into China.
sections.whyItMatters: The AI boom is blurring the intended effect of export controls: American equipment makers still expect China revenue to grow, and Chinese foundries are running at full capacity on domestic AI demand — a reminder that sanctions bite unevenly in a boom.

sections.heading: Japan's Tier IV to Design Open-Source AI Chips
sections.body: Japanese self-driving startup Tier IV plans to design open-source AI chips, Nikkei Asia reports, in a move that could lower costs and encourage automakers to bring semiconductor development in-house. The design effort is part of a broader Japanese push to build domestic chip capability, which also includes the TSMC-Sony image sensor joint venture at Kumamoto slated to begin production in 2029 — a deal Nikkei says brings overseas investment in Japan chipmaking to $37 billion.
sections.whyItMatters: Open-source chip design is a low-cost route for Japan to reduce dependence on foreign AI silicon, complementing the subsidized foundry strategy — but it remains to be seen whether open designs can match the performance of Nvidia's closed stack.

bottomLine: The day's developments center on two fronts: China's mineral leverage over Japan is now visibly biting, with heavy rare earth imports down roughly 80% and inventories being drawn down, while Washington is pushing offensive cyber capability into the private sector even as US and South Korean agencies warn of an increasingly industrialized Gunra ransomware threat. On the chip side, the AI boom continues to enrich memory makers and keep both Chinese foundries and American equipment suppliers selling into China despite export controls. The through-line is that supply-chain leverage — in minerals, memory and cyber — is being exercised more aggressively on all sides.
sources: Nikkei Asia, Reuters, BleepingComputer, Ars Technica, CISA, Vozpópuli, The Hacker News
